lessons.content_ar: مكبر الوقوف يثبت العدسة على حامل ويحافظ على مسافة محددة نسبياً بينها وبين الصفحة؛ لذلك قد يكون مناسباً لمن لديهم رعشة أو صعوبة في تثبيت المكبر اليدوي. لا يكفي اختيار القوة المكتوبة على الجهاز، بل يجب اختبار القراءة الفعلية والسرعة وفهم النص والراحة. زيادة القوة غالباً تقلل المجال المرئي ومسافة العمل. يجب تدريب المريض على وضع قاعدة الجهاز وتحقيق البؤرة ومتابعة السطور، مع تقييم الإضاءة والوهج.
lessons.content_en:
## Learning objectives
- Explain the optical design and working principle of stand magnifiers.
- Select magnification and illumination for a defined near task.
- Describe focusing, working distance and field-of-view considerations.
- Identify clinical advantages, limitations and contraindications.
- Demonstrate patient instruction and task-based verification.

## 1. Definition and optical principle
A stand magnifier is a near-vision aid mounted in a frame or housing that maintains a relatively fixed distance between the lens and the task. The support reduces the need to hold the lens at a precise distance and can improve stability for patients with tremor, reduced dexterity or limited accommodation. The magnifying effect depends on lens power, design, eye-to-lens distance and the position of the object relative to the focal plane.

## 2. Designs
Stand magnifiers may be illuminated or non-illuminated, fixed-focus or focusable, and may use conventional spherical lenses or aspheric/achromatic designs. Some are designed for spectacle use while others provide a defined viewing geometry. Built-in illumination can improve contrast, but glare and reflections must be assessed individually.

## 3. Magnification and field
Higher power generally produces a smaller usable field and shorter working distance. Nominal magnification is not a substitute for testing actual reading speed, comprehension, posture and endurance. The smallest magnification that achieves the required print size is often a useful starting point.

## 4. Clinical assessment and fitting
Establish the task, print size, duration, lighting, habitual posture, near correction, visual field and hand function. Demonstrate the device on the patient's own material. Place the base flat on the page when required, move the page or device according to its design, and ensure the focal plane is achieved. Check binocular comfort and whether the patient can locate and follow successive words.

## 5. Advantages and limitations
Advantages include stable lens-to-task distance, reduced hand demand and potential integrated lighting. Limitations include restricted field at high powers, device bulk, fixed working geometry and difficulty with some curved or uneven surfaces.

## Clinical application
For a patient with macular disease and hand tremor, compare a stand magnifier with a handheld and electronic option. Measure reading performance and ask the patient to demonstrate use independently.

## Clinical reasoning
A patient reads a single word clearly but cannot sustain a sentence. Do not assume that more power is the solution. Reassess field, line tracking, illumination, positioning and whether an electronic aid is more functional.

## Key clinical points
- A stand provides mechanical stability, not automatic correct focus.
- Test the patient's own task and environment.
- Higher power usually reduces field and working distance.
- Illumination should be comfortable, adjustable and glare-controlled.

## References
WHO. World report on vision (2019); AAO. Preferred Practice Pattern: Vision Rehabilitation; clinical low-vision rehabilitation texts.

lessons.content_en:
## Learning objectives
- Describe the role of high-addition near spectacles in low-vision care.
- Relate plus power to working distance and accommodative demand.
- Explain field-of-view, posture and binocular considerations.
- Identify suitable patients and practical limitations.
- Verify a prescription using functional near tasks.

## 1. Overview
High-addition spectacles use high plus lenses to provide enlarged retinal images for near tasks. They may be prescribed as single-vision near spectacles or incorporated into other designs. They are hands-free and can be useful when a patient needs both hands for writing, crafts or handling objects.

## 2. Optical relationships
A higher plus power requires a closer object distance for a given relaxed-eye arrangement. The approximate reciprocal relationship between dioptric power and focal distance is useful for estimation, but the final working distance also depends on vertex distance, spectacle design, refractive correction, residual accommodation and the patient's visual strategy. Do not prescribe from a simple formula alone.

## 3. Clinical assessment
Determine near acuity and critical print size, task distance, duration, posture, binocular status, convergence ability, visual field and tolerance of close working. Assess whether the patient can maintain a stable head and body position and whether the required distance is practical for daily activities.

## 4. Binocular and monocular use
Binocular high-add spectacles may be appropriate when alignment, fusion and field allow comfortable use. In some patients, monocular use can improve performance or reduce diplopia, but it sacrifices binocular field and must be individually justified. Prismatic effects and unequal visual function require careful assessment.

## 5. Advantages and limitations
They leave the hands free and can provide a relatively wide field compared with some high-power handheld devices. Limitations include very short working distance, restricted depth of field, posture strain and reduced mobility while viewing through the near spectacles.

## Clinical application
A patient with bilateral central visual loss wants to read and write for 20-minute periods. Trial an appropriate high addition with a reading stand, adequate illumination and the patient's usual materials.

## Clinical reasoning
If print is clear only when the patient adopts an uncomfortable neck-flexed posture, the prescription is not functionally successful. Consider a reading stand, alternative device or different working distance.

## Key clinical points
- Calculate an initial estimate, then verify functionally.
- Working distance and posture are central to success.
- Assess binocular comfort and field before selecting monocular use.
- Near spectacles are not intended for walking or distance mobility.

## References
AAO vision rehabilitation guidance; WHO World report on vision (2019); standard low-vision optics texts.

lessons.content_en:
## Learning objectives
- Distinguish Galilean and Keplerian telescope designs.
- Explain angular magnification and field-of-view trade-offs.
- Identify distance tasks suitable for telescopic aids.
- Describe focusing, alignment and safe-use training.
- Recognize limitations including restricted field and reduced depth perception.

## 1. Purpose
Telescopes are distance optical aids that increase the angular size of distant targets. They may support recognition of classroom boards, signs, faces or selected stationary targets. They do not restore normal vision and are not a substitute for orientation and mobility skills.

## 2. Optical designs
A Galilean telescope uses a positive objective and a negative ocular lens; it is relatively compact and provides an upright image. A Keplerian telescope uses positive objective and ocular lenses and typically requires an erecting system to provide an upright image. Design affects length, field, brightness and image quality.

## 3. Magnification and field
Angular magnification is commonly described as the ratio of the angular size seen through the telescope to that seen unaided. Increasing magnification generally narrows the field and makes target acquisition more difficult. The lowest power that meets the task is often preferred.

## 4. Assessment and fitting
Clarify the target distance, size, contrast, lighting and viewing duration. Assess acuity, field, contrast sensitivity, ocular alignment, hand control and cognitive/learning needs. Fit and focus at the intended distance and demonstrate target acquisition before independent use.

## 5. Safety and limitations
A telescope restricts peripheral awareness and may alter spatial judgement. It should not be used while walking, crossing roads or performing tasks requiring broad environmental awareness unless specifically designed and assessed for that purpose. Spotting scopes and spectacle-mounted systems have different handling demands.

## Clinical application
A school learner needs to read a board from a fixed seat. Trial a low-power telescope at the actual seat and board distance; assess speed, comfort and ability to locate the target.

## Clinical reasoning
If the learner sees the board clearly after alignment but repeatedly loses it, training and lower magnification may be more useful than increasing power.

## Key clinical points
- Telescopes are task-specific distance aids.
- Higher magnification usually narrows field and complicates acquisition.
- Teach locate-align-focus-use sequence.
- Restricted field creates important mobility and safety limitations.

## References
WHO World report on vision (2019); AAO vision rehabilitation guidance; low-vision rehabilitation optics texts.

lessons.content_ar: المكبرات الإلكترونية تستخدم كاميرا وشاشة لعرض النص أو الأشياء بحجم أكبر، وقد توفر تغيير التباين والألوان وتجميد الصورة وخط القراءة. لا يعني تكبير الصورة أكثر أن الأداء أفضل؛ فقد يقل عدد الكلمات الظاهرة وتزداد صعوبة التنقل. اختبر القراءة والفهم والراحة والبطارية وسهولة التحكم، واستفد من خصائص الوصول الموجودة في الأجهزة التي يمتلكها المريض.
lessons.content_en:
## Learning objectives
- Describe common electronic magnification platforms.
- Explain adjustable magnification, contrast and display controls.
- Match device features to visual and functional needs.
- Identify accessibility, ergonomics and cost considerations.
- Evaluate real-world task performance rather than screen enlargement alone.

## 1. Overview
Electronic magnification devices use a camera and display to enlarge text or objects. They include portable digital magnifiers, tablet-based systems, computer cameras and dedicated electronic readers. Image processing may provide contrast enhancement, polarity reversal, freeze-frame and adjustable magnification.

## 2. Core functions
Useful controls may include magnification level, brightness, contrast, colour modes, focus, reading line/curtain and image capture. Not every user benefits from every mode. High magnification can reduce the amount of material visible and increase navigation demands.

## 3. Selection
Consider the primary task, portability, screen size, battery life, camera quality, latency, controls, durability, accessibility and cost. Assess the patient's ability to operate menus, charge the device and maintain a comfortable posture. Check compatibility with existing phones, tablets or computers where appropriate.

## 4. Clinical verification
Test actual reading speed, comprehension, writing, viewing distance and fatigue. Compare natural colour, enhanced contrast and reverse polarity. Evaluate performance under the patient's usual lighting and with representative materials.

## 5. Limitations
Electronic aids may be expensive, require charging and technical support, and can introduce glare, motion delay or a learning burden. They do not replace appropriate refractive correction, lighting or rehabilitation training.

## Clinical application
A patient with reduced contrast sensitivity struggles with newspaper print. Compare a portable electronic magnifier with a tablet accessibility feature and a stand magnifier, using the same passage and task duration.

## Clinical reasoning
A larger image is not necessarily a better outcome. If the patient sees fewer words and reads more slowly, reduce magnification, change contrast or use line guidance.

## Key clinical points
- Personalize magnification and display settings.
- Assess usability, endurance and comprehension.
- Consider existing devices and accessibility settings.
- Training and follow-up are essential.

## References
WHO World report on vision (2019); W3C accessibility guidance; AAO vision rehabilitation guidance.

lessons.content_ar: نظام CCTV أو المكبر المرئي يصور الصفحة بكاميرا ويعرضها مكبرة على شاشة. قد يحتوي على طاولة متحركة XY لتسهيل تحريك الورق، مع خيارات للتباين والتركيز وخطوط القراءة. يجب تقييم القراءة والكتابة كل واحدة على حدة؛ فقد يستطيع المريض قراءة النص لكنه لا يرى يده أثناء الكتابة. راعِ مساحة الجهاز ووضعية الجلوس والوهج والتكلفة.
lessons.content_en:
## Learning objectives
- Explain the components and operation of video magnifiers.
- Identify camera, monitor and table configurations.
- Select magnification and contrast settings for near tasks.
- Recognize ergonomic and practical limitations.
- Train users to position material and navigate the viewing area.

## 1. Definition
A video magnifier, historically called a closed-circuit television (CCTV) system, captures a target with a camera and displays an enlarged image on a monitor. Modern systems may be desktop, portable or integrated with computer functions.

## 2. Components and modes
Typical components include a camera, display, controls and, in desktop systems, a movable XY table. Features may include autofocus, adjustable magnification, contrast modes, reading lines, image freeze and distance viewing. Camera-to-screen geometry and monitor size influence the usable field.

## 3. Clinical benefits
Video magnifiers can provide high magnification with adjustable contrast and may support reading, writing, medication labels, photographs and detailed tasks. The XY table can help move material systematically under the camera.

## 4. Assessment and training
Evaluate desk space, seating, posture, hand control, visual field, preferred contrast and task duration. Teach the user to place material, focus, select a comfortable magnification and move the table in controlled increments. Ensure the patient can return to the beginning of the next line.

## 5. Limitations
Desktop systems may be costly, bulky and less portable. Excessive magnification narrows the visible area. Autofocus may struggle with reflective or three-dimensional objects. Screen glare and neck or shoulder strain should be monitored.

## Clinical application
A patient needs to read mail and complete forms. Compare a desktop video magnifier with a portable unit and assess both reading and writing under realistic conditions.

## Clinical reasoning
If the user can read but cannot write because the hand and pen are not visible, adjust camera position, display configuration or select a system with a suitable writing mode.

## Key clinical points
- Evaluate reading and writing separately.
- Train XY table control and line navigation.
- Optimize ergonomics and screen position.
- Confirm the device fits the user's home and task needs.

## References
WHO World report on vision (2019); AAO vision rehabilitation guidance; assistive technology rehabilitation texts.

lessons.content_en:
## Learning objectives
- Identify built-in accessibility features relevant to low vision.
- Distinguish magnification, screen reading and display adaptation.
- Configure digital content for an individual's functional needs.
- Address compatibility, privacy and digital literacy.
- Develop a practical training and support plan.

## 1. Concept
Digital accessibility enables people with visual impairment to access information and technology. Features may be built into operating systems, applications, browsers and websites, or supplied by specialized assistive software.

## 2. Key features
Screen magnification enlarges interface content; screen readers provide spoken output; text-to-speech reads selected text; contrast and colour settings alter presentation; cursor enlargement and focus indicators improve tracking. Optical character recognition (OCR) converts printed or image-based text into machine-readable text, but accuracy must be checked.

## 3. Accessible content
Use scalable text, clear headings, meaningful labels, sufficient contrast and logical reading order. Avoid conveying information by colour alone. Images require useful alternative text when they convey information. PDF files should contain selectable text and a logical structure where possible.

## 4. Clinical matching
Determine whether the person primarily needs enlarged visual access, auditory access or a combination. Consider hearing, language, cognition, dexterity, device familiarity and internet availability. Demonstrate settings using the patient's own phone or computer.

## 5. Risks and limitations
Features vary by platform and application. Poorly structured documents may remain inaccessible despite magnification. Speech output may be unsuitable in noisy or private environments. Protect personal information when using cloud services and shared devices.

## Clinical application
A university student with low vision must read digital lecture notes. Configure scalable text, high contrast or text-to-speech as preferred, and test navigation through headings and tables.

## Clinical reasoning
If magnification causes horizontal scrolling and loss of context, consider reflowable text, a larger display, OCR with speech output or a hybrid approach.

## Key clinical points
- Choose features according to the task and user preference.
- Check document structure, not just font size.
- Teach the user to enable and customize settings.
- Review privacy, compatibility and ongoing support.

## References
W3C Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG); WHO World report on vision (2019); platform accessibility documentation.

lessons.content_ar: المعينات غير البصرية لا تعتمد أساساً على العدسات المكبرة؛ بل تغير البيئة أو طريقة أداء المهمة. أمثلتها الإضاءة المناسبة، الأقلام ذات الخط العريض، الورق المسطر بوضوح، العلامات اللمسية، الساعات الناطقة والكتب الصوتية. في المهام الحساسة مثل تمييز الأدوية لا تعتمد على اللون وحده، بل استخدم نظاماً آمناً موثوقاً وتدريباً مناسباً.
lessons.content_en:
## Learning objectives
- Classify common non-optical low-vision aids.
- Explain how contrast, lighting and tactile cues support function.
- Match aids to daily living and mobility tasks.
- Identify environmental and safety considerations.
- Incorporate patient preference into rehabilitation planning.

## 1. Definition
Non-optical aids improve function without relying primarily on magnifying lenses. They modify the task, environment, sensory cues or organization of activities. They complement optical and electronic devices.

## 2. Examples
Examples include task lighting, bold-line paper, felt-tip pens, large-print materials, tactile labels, talking clocks, audio books, high-contrast markings, signature guides, large-button phones and liquid-level indicators. Selection depends on the activity and the user's abilities.

## 3. Contrast and illumination
High contrast can make edges and objects easier to detect, but glare must be controlled. Appropriate task lighting should be adjustable and positioned to avoid reflections. Colour choices should be tested rather than assumed to work equally for all patients.

## 4. Daily living and safety
Mark stair edges, identify medication containers using safe systems, organize household items consistently and use tactile or auditory cues where helpful. Medication identification must be reliable; colour alone is not a safe method. Occupational therapy input may be valuable.

## 5. Assessment and training
Ask which activities are difficult and observe the person performing them. Introduce aids one at a time, demonstrate use and confirm that the strategy is safe and sustainable.

## Clinical application
An older adult has difficulty identifying controls on a cooker. Consider tactile markers, high-contrast labels and an occupational therapy safety assessment.

## Clinical reasoning
A bright lamp may improve detail but worsen glare. Adjust direction, diffusion and task contrast rather than simply increasing brightness.

## Key clinical points
- Non-optical strategies can produce major functional gains.
- Safety-critical tasks require reliable identification methods.
- Observe real activities and train the patient.
- Combine environmental changes with optical aids when appropriate.

## References
WHO World report on vision (2019); low-vision rehabilitation and occupational therapy guidance.

lessons.content_en:
## Learning objectives
- Define eccentric viewing and its rehabilitation purpose.
- Explain why central scotoma may interfere with fixation and reading.
- Describe the principles of locating a usable retinal area.
- Outline structured training and functional evaluation.
- Recognize individual variability and limitations.

## 1. Definition
Eccentric viewing is a learned visual strategy in which a person with central visual loss directs gaze so that an area of functioning retina outside the damaged foveal region is used to view a target. It may help with recognition of faces, objects or text when central fixation is ineffective.

## 2. Rationale
Macular disease can produce a central scotoma that obscures the target during direct fixation. A peripheral or parafoveal retinal area may provide a more useful view, although acuity, sensitivity and stability are usually different from normal foveal function.

## 3. Training principles
Training begins with assessment of the visual field and fixation behaviour, often using appropriate clinical instruments. The clinician helps the patient explore gaze positions and identify a direction that gives the most stable and useful image. Training progresses from simple stationary targets to more complex functional tasks.

## 4. Functional practice
Practice may include locating a high-contrast target, recognizing objects, viewing faces and attempting reading. Reading requires additional skills such as sequential eye movements, line transitions and maintaining the preferred viewing direction. A strategy effective for one task may not transfer automatically to another.

## 5. Limitations
Not every patient develops a stable or effective eccentric viewing strategy. Results depend on retinal disease, scotoma characteristics, cognition, motivation and training. Avoid promising restoration of normal central vision.

## Clinical application
A patient with bilateral central scotomas has difficulty recognizing faces. Assess fixation and field, identify a potentially useful retinal area and practice target recognition with appropriate lighting and contrast.

## Clinical reasoning
If a gaze direction helps object detection but worsens reading, use task-specific assessment rather than assuming one preferred direction works for every activity.

## Key clinical points
- Eccentric viewing is a compensatory learned strategy.
- Identify a usable retinal area through assessment and practice.
- Train task-specific performance.
- It does not reverse macular pathology or restore the fovea.

## References
AAO vision rehabilitation guidance; WHO World report on vision (2019); macular rehabilitation literature.

lessons.content_ar: الموضع الشبكي المفضل PRL هو منطقة شبكية خارج النقرة اعتاد المريض استخدامها للتثبيت بعد فقدان الرؤية المركزية. قد يتكون تلقائياً وقد يختلف بين العينين أو بين المهام. لا يكفي قياس حدة البصر لتحديده؛ يمكن تقييم ثبات التثبيت والمجال والأداء الوظيفي، وقد تساعد تقنية microperimetry عند توفرها. وجود PRL ثابت لا يضمن قراءة طليقة.
lessons.content_en:
## Learning objectives
- Define the preferred retinal locus (PRL).
- Differentiate an established PRL from a trained eccentric viewing strategy.
- Describe factors affecting PRL location and stability.
- Explain clinical assessment and rehabilitation implications.
- Interpret PRL limitations in reading and visual tasks.

## 1. Definition
The preferred retinal locus is a retinal area outside the damaged fovea that a person habitually uses for fixation after central vision loss. It may develop spontaneously and can differ between individuals and between eyes.

## 2. Development and characteristics
A PRL may emerge as the visual system adapts to a central scotoma. Its location, size, sensitivity and stability influence functional performance. Some patients have more than one locus or use different areas for different tasks.

## 3. Assessment
Assessment may include fixation observation, visual field testing and microperimetry where available. Evaluate stability, direction of eccentric gaze, reading performance and functional vision. A PRL should not be assumed from acuity alone.

## 4. Rehabilitation
Training may aim to improve awareness and use of an existing locus or develop a more functional strategy. The optimal location is not necessarily identical for all tasks. Reading may require a locus and eye movement pattern that support sequential text processing.

## 5. Clinical interpretation
A stable PRL may improve target localization but does not guarantee fluent reading. Reduced contrast sensitivity, crowding, field loss and impaired eye movement control can remain limiting factors.

## Clinical application
A patient with geographic atrophy demonstrates eccentric fixation. Document the observed locus and test whether it supports face recognition, object finding and reading separately.

## Clinical reasoning
Do not label every eccentric fixation point as an optimal PRL. Confirm repeatability and functional benefit, and consider referral for specialized microperimetry if available.

## Key clinical points
- PRL is an individual's habitual eccentric fixation area.
- It may be spontaneous and is not always optimal.
- Stability and task performance both matter.
- Assess each important visual task independently.

## References
Macular rehabilitation literature; AAO vision rehabilitation guidance; WHO World report on vision (2019).

lessons.content_ar: تأهيل القراءة يتطلب تقييم حدة القراءة وحجم الطباعة الحرج والسرعة والدقة والفهم، وليس مجرد معرفة أصغر حرف يستطيع المريض رؤيته. قد تشمل التدخلات النظارات القريبة والمكبرات والأجهزة الإلكترونية والطباعة الكبيرة وتحويل النص إلى صوت. يجب ضبط الإضاءة والتباين والوضعية واستخدام دليل للسطور عند الحاجة. نجاح التدخل يقاس بالسرعة والفهم والتحمل وتحقيق هدف المريض.
lessons.content_en:
## Learning objectives
- Identify visual and non-visual determinants of reading performance.
- Select optical, electronic and non-optical reading strategies.
- Explain the role of print size, contrast, illumination and field.
- Design task-specific reading practice and monitor outcomes.
- Address comprehension, fatigue, posture and environmental barriers.

## 1. Reading as a functional task
Reading requires adequate resolution, contrast, visual span, fixation, eye movements, language and cognition. A patient may recognize isolated letters yet struggle with continuous text because of crowding, central scotoma, reduced field or impaired tracking.

## 2. Assessment
Record reading acuity, critical print size, reading speed, accuracy and comprehension using appropriate standardized or repeatable materials. Ask about preferred materials, language, duration, lighting and real-life goals. Assess posture, working distance, fatigue and the impact of ocular and systemic conditions.

## 3. Intervention options
Options include updated refractive correction, appropriate near addition, handheld or stand magnifiers, high-add spectacles, electronic magnifiers, large print, screen magnification, text-to-speech and audiobooks. Select by demonstrated performance rather than device category alone.

## 4. Environmental optimization
Provide comfortable task illumination, reduce glare, increase contrast and use a stable reading surface. Reading stands may improve posture. Line guides, typoscopes and spacing adjustments may support place-keeping.

## 5. Training and outcomes
Teach device handling, focusing, scanning and line transitions. Use short, progressive practice sessions and monitor reading speed, comprehension, endurance and confidence. Involve family, educators or rehabilitation professionals with the patient's consent.

## Clinical application
A patient with macular disease wants to read medication instructions and messages. Establish print-size needs and compare optical, electronic and auditory approaches; ensure medication information is accessed safely.

## Clinical reasoning
If reading speed improves but comprehension falls, the intervention has not fully met the goal. Adjust magnification, text layout or use speech support and reassess.

## Key clinical points
- Reading speed and comprehension must both be measured.
- The best device is the one that supports the patient's real goal.
- Optimize posture, illumination and contrast.
- Training and follow-up are part of the intervention.

## References
WHO World report on vision (2019); AAO vision rehabilitation guidance; standardized low-vision reading assessment literature.
